claim: A diallel panel of 3025 yeast hybrids was generated from pairwise crosses between 55 natural isolates.
source: Based on the genomic and phenotypic data from the 1,011 S. cerevisiae isolate collection (Peter et al., 2018), we selected a subset of 55 isolates that were diploid, homozygous, genetically diverse (Figure 1a), and originated from a broad range of ecological sources (Figure 1b) (e.g. tree exudates, Drosophila, fruits, fermentation processes, clinical isolates) as well as geographical origins (Europe, America, Africa and Asia) (Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1). A full diallel cross panel was constructed by systematically crossing the 55 selected isolates in a pairwise manner (Figure 1d). In total, we generated 3025 hybrids, representing 2970 heterozygous hybrids with a unique parental combination and 55 homozygous hybrids.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and reports the number of hybrids generated from the diallel cross.

claim: All 3025 hybrids were viable, indicating no dominant lethal interactions existed between the parental isolates.
source: All 3025 hybrids were viable, indicating no dominant lethal interactions existed between the parental isolates.
evidence: The manuscript reports the observation that all hybrids were viable.

claim: The diallel panel was phenotyped across 49 growth conditions that induce various physiological and cellular responses.
source: We then screened the entire set of the parental isolates and hybrids for quantification of mitotic growth abilities across 49 conditions that induce various physiological and cellular responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phenotyping experiment and references figures showing the conditions tested.

claim: The phenotyping step led to the characterization of 148,225 hybrid/trait combinations.
source: Ultimately, this phenotyping step led to the characterization of 148,225 hybrid/trait combinations.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of hybrid/trait combinations characterized.

claim: The 55 selected isolates were diploid, homozygous, and genetically diverse.
source: Based on the genomic and phenotypic data from the 1,011 S. cerevisiae isolate collection (Peter et al., 2018), we selected a subset of 55 isolates that were diploid, homozygous, genetically diverse (Figure 1a), and originated from a broad range of ecological sources (Figure 1b) (e.g. tree exudates, Drosophila, fruits, fermentation processes, clinical isolates) as well as geographical origins (Europe, America, Africa and Asia) (Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the selection criteria for the parental isolates and references a figure showing genetic diversity.

claim: The selected isolates originated from a broad range of ecological sources including tree exudates, Drosophila, fruits, fermentation processes, and clinical isolates.
source: Based on the genomic and phenotypic data from the 1,011 S. cerevisiae isolate collection (Peter et al., 2018), we selected a subset of 55 isolates that were diploid, homozygous, genetically diverse (Figure 1a), and originated from a broad range of ecological sources (Figure 1b) (e.g. tree exudates, Drosophila, fruits, fermentation processes, clinical isolates) as well as geographical origins (Europe, America, Africa and Asia) (Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript lists the ecological sources of the selected isolates and references a figure showing this information.

claim: The selected isolates originated from geographical origins including Europe, America, Africa and Asia.
source: Based on the genomic and phenotypic data from the 1,011 S. cerevisiae isolate collection (Peter et al., 2018), we selected a subset of 55 isolates that were diploid, homozygous, genetically diverse (Figure 1a), and originated from a broad range of ecological sources (Figure 1b) (e.g. tree exudates, Drosophila, fruits, fermentation processes, clinical isolates) as well as geographical origins (Europe, America, Africa and Asia) (Figure 1c and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript lists the geographical origins and references a figure showing this information.

claim: Broad-sense heritability (H2) values for each condition ranged from 0.64 to 0.98.
source: The H2 values for each condition ranged from 0.64 to 0.98, with the lowest value observed for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of H2 values calculated from the diallel analysis.

claim: The lowest broad-sense heritability value was observed for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1).
source: The H2 values for each condition ranged from 0.64 to 0.98, with the lowest value observed for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the condition with the lowest H2 value.

claim: The highest broad-sense heritability value was observed for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM).
source: The H2 values for each condition ranged from 0.64 to 0.98, with the lowest value observed for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the condition with the highest H2 value.

claim: Narrow-sense heritability (h2) values ranged from 0.12 to 0.86.
source: The additive part (h2 values) ranged from 0.12 to 0.86, with the lowest value for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of h2 values calculated from the diallel analysis.

claim: The lowest narrow-sense heritability value was observed for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1).
source: The additive part (h2 values) ranged from 0.12 to 0.86, with the lowest value for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the condition with the lowest h2 value.

claim: The highest narrow-sense heritability value was observed for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM).
source: The additive part (h2 values) ranged from 0.12 to 0.86, with the lowest value for fluconazole (1 µg.ml−1) and the highest for sodium meta-arsenite (2.5 mM), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript identifies the condition with the highest h2 value.

claim: On average, most of the phenotypic variance can be explained by additive effects (mean h2 = 0.55).
source: While broad- and narrow-sense heritabilities are variable across conditions, we also observed that on average, most of the phenotypic variance can be explained by additive effects (mean h2 = 0.55).
evidence: The manuscript reports the mean narrow-sense heritability across all conditions.

claim: Non-additive components contribute significantly to some traits, explaining on average one third of the phenotypic variance observed (mean H2 - h2 = 0.29).
source: However, non-additive components contribute significantly to some traits, explaining on average one third of the phenotypic variance observed (mean H2 - h2 = 0.29) (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the mean contribution of non-additive effects calculated from the difference between H2 and h2.

claim: There is a good correlation between broad- and narrow-sense heritabilities (Pearson's r = 0.809, p-value=1.921e-12).
source: Despite a good correlation between broad- and narrow-sense heritabilities (Pearson's r = 0.809, p-value=1.921e-12) (Figure 2c), some traits display a larger non-additive contribution, such as in galactose (2%) or ketoconazole (10 µg/ml).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation coefficient and p-value from statistical analysis.

claim: Some traits display a larger non-additive contribution, such as in galactose (2%) or ketoconazole (10 µg/ml).
source: Despite a good correlation between broad- and narrow-sense heritabilities (Pearson's r = 0.809, p-value=1.921e-12) (Figure 2c), some traits display a larger non-additive contribution, such as in galactose (2%) or ketoconazole (10 µg/ml).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific conditions with larger non-additive contributions.

claim: Galactose (2%) and ketoconazole (10 µg/ml) conditions are mainly controlled by dominance.
source: Interestingly, we revealed that these two conditions revealed to be mainly controlled by dominance (see below).
evidence: The manuscript states that these conditions are controlled by dominance based on further analysis.

claim: Additive effects play a main role in shaping complex traits at a population-scale.
source: Altogether, our results highlight the main role of additive effects in shaping complex traits at a population-scale and clearly show that this is not restricted to the single yeast cross where this trend was first observed (Bloom et al., 2013; Bloom et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the heritability results and cites previous studies showing similar trends.

claim: The extensive impact of non-additive effects on phenotypic variance is corroborated at a species-wide level.
source: This result also corroborates at a species-wide level the extensive impact of non-additive effects on phenotypic variance (Forsberg et al., 2017; Yadav et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing non-additive effects and states that the current results corroborate these findings.

claim: Only 17.4% of all hybrid/condition combinations showed enough phenotypic separation between the parents and the corresponding hybrid to allow complete partitioning into seven modes of inheritance.
source: Only 17.4% of all hybrid/condition combinations showed enough phenotypic separation between the parents and the corresponding hybrid, allowing the complete partitioning in the seven above-mentioned modes of inheritance.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of cases where complete mode of inheritance classification was possible.

claim: For 82.6% of cases, only a separation of overdominance and underdominance can be achieved.
source: For the 82.6% remaining cases, only a separation of overdominance and underdominance can be achieved (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of cases where only partial classification was possible.

claim: 11.6% of hybrid/condition combinations showed overdominance.
source: Interestingly, these events are not as rare as previously described (Zörgö et al., 2012), with 11.6% of overdominance and 10.1% of underdominance (Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of overdominance cases and cites a previous study for comparison.

claim: 10.1% of hybrid/condition combinations showed underdominance.
source: Interestingly, these events are not as rare as previously described (Zörgö et al., 2012), with 11.6% of overdominance and 10.1% of underdominance (Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of underdominance cases and cites a previous study for comparison.

claim: When a clear separation is possible, one third of the condition/cross combinations detected were purely additive.
source: When a clear separation is possible (Figure 3e), one third of the condition/cross combinations detected were purely additive whereas the rest displayed a deviation towards one of the two parents, with no bias (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of additive cases when clear separation is possible.

claim: When a clear separation is possible, the rest of the condition/cross combinations displayed a deviation towards one of the two parents, with no bias.
source: When a clear separation is possible (Figure 3e), one third of the condition/cross combinations detected were purely additive whereas the rest displayed a deviation towards one of the two parents, with no bias (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of non-additive cases and notes the lack of bias.

claim: Most of the studied growth conditions (32 out of 49) showed a prevalence of additive effects.
source: When looking at the inheritance mode in each condition, most of the studied growth conditions (32 out of 49) showed a prevalence of additive effects (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of conditions showing predominantly additive effects.

claim: 17 conditions were not predominantly additive throughout the population.
source: However, 17 conditions were not predominantly additive throughout the population.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of conditions not showing predominantly additive effects.

claim: A total of 12 conditions were detected as mostly dominant with 4 cases of best parent dominance and 8 of worst parent dominance.
source: Indeed, a total of 12 conditions were detected as mostly dominant with 4 cases of best parent dominance, including galactose (2%) and ketoconazole (10 µg.ml−1), and 8 of worst parent dominance.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of conditions showing dominance and breaks down the types of dominance.

claim: Five conditions displayed a majority of partial dominance.
source: The remaining five conditions displayed a majority of partial dominance (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of conditions showing partial dominance.

claim: Dominance plays a major role as a driver for non-additive effects.
source: These results confirm the importance of additivity in the global architecture of traits, but more importantly, they clearly demonstrate the major role of dominance as a driver for non-additive effects.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the mode of inheritance results to conclude about the role of dominance.

claim: The presence of conditions with a high proportion of partial dominance combined with cases of over and underdominance may indicate a strong and pervasive impact of epistasis on phenotypic variation.
source: Nevertheless, the presence of conditions with a high proportion of partial dominance combined with the cases of over and underdominance may indicate a strong and pervasive impact of epistasis on phenotypic variation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the role of epistasis based on the observed patterns of inheritance.

claim: A subset of hybrids from 34 unrelated isolates was selected to perform GWAS to avoid issues due to population structure.
source: To avoid issues due to population structure, we selected a subset of hybrids from 34 unrelated isolates in the original panel to perform GWAS (see Materials and methods, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the selection of a subset for GWAS analysis.

claim: 595 hybrid genotypes were constructed in silico by combining known parental genomes.
source: By combining known parental genomes, we constructed 595 hybrid genotypes in silico, matching one half matrix of the diallel plus the 34 homozygous diploids.
evidence: The manuscript describes the construction of hybrid genotypes for GWAS.

claim: A total of 31,632 polymorphic sites remained after filtering SNPs to retain biallelic variants with no missing calls and removing extensive long-distance linkage disequilibrium.
source: We built a matrix of genetic variants for this panel and filtered SNPs to only retain biallelic variants with no missing calls. In addition, due to the small number of unique parental genotypes, extensive long-distance linkage disequilibrium was also removed (see Materials and methods), leaving a total of 31,632 polymorphic sites in the diallel population.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering process and reports the final number of SNPs.

claim: 3.8% (a total of 1,180 SNPs) had a MAF lower than 0.05 in the initial population but surpassed this threshold in the diallel panel, reaching a MAF of 0.32.
source: Overall, 3.8% (a total of 1,180 SNPs) had a MAF lower than 0.05 in the initial population of the 1,011 S. cerevisiae isolates but surpassed this threshold in the diallel panel, reaching a MAF of 0.32 (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage and number of SNPs that increased in frequency in the diallel panel.

claim: GWAS revealed 1723 significantly associated SNPs.
source: Overall, GWAS revealed 1723 significantly associated SNPs (Figure 4—source data 1) by detecting from 2 to 103 significant SNPs by condition, with an average of 39 SNPs per condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of significantly associated SNPs from GWAS.

claim: GWAS detected from 2 to 103 significant SNPs by condition, with an average of 39 SNPs per condition.
source: Overall, GWAS revealed 1723 significantly associated SNPs (Figure 4—source data 1) by detecting from 2 to 103 significant SNPs by condition, with an average of 39 SNPs per condition.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range and average number of significant SNPs per condition.

claim: 16.3% of the significant SNPs (281 in total) corresponded to low-frequency variants (MAF <0.05).
source: Interestingly, 16.3% of the significant SNPs (281 in total) corresponded to low-frequency variants (MAF <0.05), with 19.5% of them (55 SNPs) being rare variants (MAF <0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage and number of low-frequency variants among significant SNPs.

claim: 19.5% of the low-frequency significant SNPs (55 SNPs) were rare variants (MAF <0.01).
source: Interestingly, 16.3% of the significant SNPs (281 in total) corresponded to low-frequency variants (MAF <0.05), with 19.5% of them (55 SNPs) being rare variants (MAF <0.01).
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage and number of rare variants among low-frequency significant SNPs.

claim: The trend of low-frequency variant enrichment is maintained for both additive and overdominant models, with 19.3% and 15.2% of low-frequency variants respectively.
source: This trend is the same and maintained for both models, with 19.3% and 15.2% of low-frequency variants for the additive and overdominant models, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentages of low-frequency variants for each encoding model.

claim: Low-frequency variants indeed play a significant part in the phenotypic variance at the population-scale.
source: However, these results clearly show that low-frequency variants indeed play a significant part in the phenotypic variance at the population-scale.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the GWAS results to conclude about the role of low-frequency variants.

claim: Detected SNPs could explain 15% to 32% of the variance, with a median of 20%.
source: We then estimated the contribution of the significant variants to total phenotypic variation (see Materials and methods) in our panel and found that detected SNPs could explained 15% to 32% of the variance, with a median of 20% (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the range and median of variance explained by detected SNPs.

claim: Low-frequency variants explained roughly the same proportion of the phenotypic variation (median of 20.2%) as common SNPs (median of 19.6%).
source: When looking at the variance explained by each variant over their respective allele frequency, it is noteworthy that low-frequency variants explained roughly the same proportion of the phenotypic variation (median of 20.2%) than the common SNPs (median of 19.6%) (Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript reports the median variance explained by low-frequency and common variants.

claim: The variance explained by the associated rare variants was higher on average than the rest of the detected SNPs.
source: In addition, the variance explained by the associated rare variants were also higher on average than the rest of the detected SNPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the comparison of variance explained by rare variants versus other SNPs.

claim: The trend of rare variants explaining more variance is robust and conserved across the two encoding models implemented, accounting for additive and overdominant effects.
source: It is noteworthy that this trend was robust and conserved across the two encoding models implemented, accounting for additive and overdominant effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the trend holds across different models.

claim: On average, low-frequency variants have about the same effect size (mean of 0.23 sd) as common variants (mean of 0.25 sd).
source: Here again we found that on average, low-frequency variant have about the same effect size (mean of 0.23 sd) than the common variants (mean of 0.25 sd).
evidence: The manuscript reports the mean effect sizes for low-frequency and common variants.

claim: 62.5% of the associated SNPs are in coding regions.
source: To gain insight into the biological relevance of the set of associated SNPs, we first examined their distribution across the genome and found that 62.5% of them are in coding regions (with coding regions representing a total of 72.9% of the S. cerevisiae genome) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), with all of these SNPs distributed over a set of 546 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of associated SNPs in coding regions.

claim: Coding regions represent a total of 72.9% of the S. cerevisiae genome.
source: To gain insight into the biological relevance of the set of associated SNPs, we first examined their distribution across the genome and found that 62.5% of them are in coding regions (with coding regions representing a total of 72.9% of the S. cerevisiae genome) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), with all of these SNPs distributed over a set of 546 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of the genome that is coding.

claim: The associated SNPs are distributed over a set of 546 genes.
source: To gain insight into the biological relevance of the set of associated SNPs, we first examined their distribution across the genome and found that 62.5% of them are in coding regions (with coding regions representing a total of 72.9% of the S. cerevisiae genome) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), with all of these SNPs distributed over a set of 546 genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genes containing associated SNPs.

claim: 19 of the genes detected are included in a list of 145 quantitative trait genes (QTG) identified over the last decade.
source: Over the last decade, an impressive number of quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping experiments were performed on a myriad of phenotypes in yeast leading to the identification of 145 quantitative trait genes (QTG) (Peltier et al., 2019) and we found that 19 of the genes we detected are included in this list (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript compares the detected genes with a list of known QTGs from a cited study.

claim: 22 associated genes overlap with a recent large-scale linkage mapping survey in yeast.
source: In addition, 22 associated genes were also found as overlapping with a recent large-scale linkage mapping survey in yeast (Bloom et al., 2019) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The manuscript compares the detected genes with results from a cited study.

claim: The associated genes are enriched for genes involved in 'response to stimulus' and 'response to stress' (p-value=5.39×10−5).
source: This analysis revealed an enrichment (p-value=5.39×10−5) in genes involved in 'response to stimulus' and 'response to stress', which is in line with the different tested conditions leading to various physiological and cellular responses.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: A low-frequency variant in the SGD1 gene was detected in 6-azauracile (100 µg.ml−1) with a p-value of 2.75e-8 with the overdominant encoding and 6.26e-5 with the additive encoding.
source: The chosen variant was characterized by two adjacent SNPs in the SGD1 gene and was detected in 6-azauracile (100 µg.ml−1) with a p-value of 2.75e-8 with the overdominant encoding and 6.26e-5 with the additive encoding.
evidence: The manuscript reports the detection of a specific variant with associated p-values.

claim: The MAF of the SGD1 variant in the initial population is only 2.5% and reached 9% in the diallel panel.
source: Their MAF in the initial population is only 2.5% and reached 9% in the diallel panel with three genetically distant strains carrying it (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the MAF of the SGD1 variant in both populations.

claim: Three genetically distant strains carry the SGD1 minor allele.
source: Their MAF in the initial population is only 2.5% and reached 9% in the diallel panel with three genetically distant strains carrying it (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of strains carrying the variant.

claim: The SGD1 SNPs are in the coding sequence of SGD1, an essential gene encoding a nuclear protein.
source: The SNPs are in the coding sequence of SGD1, an essential gene encoding a nuclear protein.
evidence: The manuscript describes the location and function of the gene containing the variant.

claim: The minor allele (AA) of SGD1 induces a synonymous change (TTG (Leu) → TTA (Leu)) for the first position and a non-synonymous mutation (GAA (Glu)→ AAA (Lys)) for the second position.
source: The minor allele (AA) induces a synonymous change (TTG (Leu) → TTA (Leu)) for the first position and a non-synonymous mutation (GAA (Glu)→ AAA (Lys)) for the second position (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the molecular consequences of the variant.

claim: The phenotypic advantage conferred by the SGD1 minor allele was observed with a significant difference between the homozygous for the minor allele, heterozygous and homozygous for the major allele.
source: The phenotypic advantage conferred by this allele was observed with a significant difference between the homozygous for the minor allele, heterozygous and homozygous for the major allele (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the phenotypic differences between genotypes.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing was used to switch the SGD1 minor allele (AA) to the major allele (GG) in the three strains carrying the minor allele.
source: To functionally validate the phenotypic effect of this low-frequency variant, CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing was used in the three strains carrying the minor allele (AA) in order to switch it to the major allele (GG) and assess its phenotypic impact.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental validation approach.

claim: The SGD1 minor allele confers a phenotypic advantage of 0.2 in growth ratio compared to the major allele.
source: When phenotyping the wildtype strains containing the minor allele and the mutated strains with the major allele, we observed that the minor allele confers a phenotypic advantage of 0.2 in growth ratio compared to the major allele (Figure 5c) therefore validating the important phenotypic impact of this low-frequency variant.
evidence: The manuscript reports the phenotypic difference observed in the validation experiment.

claim: An important part of the phenotypic variance is linked to additive effects, while about a third remains ruled by non-additive interactions encompassing dominance and epistasis.
source: While our analysis revealed that an important part of the phenotypic variance is linked to additive effects, about a third remains ruled by non-additive interactions encompassing dominance and epistasis.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings about additive and non-additive effects.

claim: A strong enrichment in low-frequency variants has been observed in the significantly associated SNPs (16%), demonstrating the ubiquity of low-frequency variants with important phenotypic impact.
source: Although few low-frequency and rare variants were considered in our GWAS (4%) due to stringent filtering conditions, a strong enrichment in these variants has been observed in the significantly associated ones (16%), demonstrating the ubiquity of low-frequency variants with important phenotypic impact.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the enrichment of low-frequency variants among significant SNPs.

claim: At the population level, low-frequency variants have effect sizes similar to common variants but do not explain an important part of variance because variance relies both on effect size and allele frequency.
source: However, when looking at the population level, even though they do have effect sizes similar to common variants, they are not going to explain an important part of variance because it relies both on effect size and allele frequency.
evidence: The manuscript explains the relationship between effect size, allele frequency, and variance explained.

claim: A study of human height in more than 700,000 individuals mapped 83 significantly associated rare and low-frequency variants with effect sizes up to 2 cm.
source: A good example of this phenomenon has been seen with a study of human height in more than 700,000 individuals. A total of 83 significantly associated rare and low-frequency variants with effect sizes up to 2 cm have been mapped (Marouli et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on human height to illustrate the phenomenon.

claim: In the human height study, rare and low-frequency variants explained the same amount of phenotypic variation as common variants on average, despite common variants having much smaller effect sizes of about 1 mm.
source: On average, they explained the same amount of phenotypic variation as common variants, which displayed much smaller effect sizes of about 1 mm.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from a human height study.

claim: A high number of low-frequency variants play a decisive role in the phenotypic landscape of a population both in term of number and effect size.
source: Our results suggest that a high number of low-frequency variants play a decisive role in the phenotypic landscape of a population both in term of number and effect size.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the results to make a conclusion about low-frequency variants.

claim: Taken one by one, low-frequency variants do not explain a lot of phenotypic variance in a large population, but altogether, they might actually explain a greater part of the variation than the one explained by common variants.
source: Taken one by one, they do not explain a lot of phenotypic variance in a large population. Yet, altogether, they might actually explain a greater part of the variation than the one explained by common variants.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the collective contribution of low-frequency variants.

claim: The missing heritability of height and body mass index is accounted for by rare variants.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the missing heritability of height and body mass index is accounted for by rare variants (Wainschtein et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study on missing heritability.

claim: Most of the previously identified Quantitative Trait Nucleotides (QTNs) using linkage mapping were at low allele frequency in the 1,011 S. cerevisiae population.
source: We also recently found in yeast that most of the previously identified Quantitative Trait Nucleotides (QTNs) using linkage mapping were at low allele frequency in the 1,011 S. cerevisiae population (Hou et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2019; Peltier et al., 2019; Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing that QTNs are at low frequency.

claim: A total of 284 QTNs were identified by linkage mapping and 150 of them are present at a low frequency in the population of 1011 isolates.
source: A total of 284 QTNs were identified by linkage mapping and 150 of them are present at a low frequency in the population of 1011 isolates (Peltier et al., 2019; Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies reporting the number of QTNs and their frequencies.

claim: The QTNs were mapped with mostly closely related genetic backgrounds, encompassing a total of 59 strains with 30% from laboratory and 41% from the wine cluster.
source: However, these QTNs were mapped with mostly closely related genetic backgrounds, encompassing a total of 59 strains with 30% of them coming from laboratory and 41% coming from the wine cluster, which has a very low genetic diversity (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genetic backgrounds used in previous QTN mapping studies.

claim: Experimentally validated QTNs are, most of the time, genetic variants with the most important phenotypic impact, which induces an ascertainment bias.
source: Moreover, experimentally validated QTNs are, most of the time, genetic variants with the most important phenotypic impact, which has been previously recognized as inducing an ascertainment bias (Rockman, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study discussing ascertainment bias in QTN validation.

claim: Among all the genetic variants detected by GWAS on a diallel panel, 16.3% of them have a low-frequency in the initial population and explain a significant part of the phenotypic variance (21% on average).
source: Here, we quantified the contribution of low-frequency variants across a large number of growth conditions and found that among all the genetic variants detected by GWAS on a diallel panel, 16.3% of them have a low-frequency in the initial population and explain a significant part of the phenotypic variance (21% on average).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings about low-frequency variants from GWAS.

claim: The diallel design presents an intrinsic power to evaluate the additive vs. non-additive genetic components contributing to the phenotypic variation.
source: This particular diallel design also presents an intrinsic power to evaluate the additive vs. non-additive genetic components contributing to the phenotypic variation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the advantages of the diallel design.

claim: Dominance at the single locus level contributed to the phenotypic variation observed.
source: We assessed the effect of intra-locus dominance on the non-additive genetic component and showed that dominance at the single locus level contributed to the phenotypic variation observed.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings about dominance effects.

claim: Other more complicated inter-loci interactions may still be involved in phenotypic variation.
source: However, other more complicated inter-loci interactions may still be involved.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the potential role of epistasis.

claim: The study highlights the extensive role of low-frequency variants on the phenotypic variation.
source: Altogether, these results have major implications for our understanding of the genetic architecture of traits in the context of unexplained heritability. In parallel to a recent large-scale linkage mapping survey in yeast (Bloom et al., 2019), our study highlights the extensive role of low-frequency variants on the phenotypic variation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main conclusion of the study and cites a parallel study.

claim: 92.7% of the polymorphic sites in the 1011 yeast genomes dataset are associated with a minor allele frequency (MAF) lower than 0.05.
source: Interestingly, much of the detected genetic polymorphisms in the 1011 yeast genomes dataset are low-frequency variants with almost 92.7% of the polymorphic sites associated with a minor allele frequency (MAF) lower than 0.05.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of low-frequency variants in the 1011 genomes dataset.

claim: The trend of low-frequency variants is similar to that observed in the human population.
source: This trend is similar to that observed in the human population (Auton et al., 2015; Walter et al., 2015) and definitely raised a question regarding the impact of low-frequency variants on the phenotypic landscape within a population and on the missing heritability (Zuk et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript compares the yeast findings to human population genetics studies.

claim: Human height is estimated to be 60–80% heritable.
source: This trait is estimated to be 60–80% heritable (Speed et al., 2017; Visscher et al., 2008) but close to 700 variants found in an analysis based on more than 250,000 individuals only explain 20% of this total heritability (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the heritability of human height.

claim: Close to 700 variants found in an analysis based on more than 250,000 individuals only explain 20% of the total heritability of human height.
source: This trait is estimated to be 60–80% heritable (Speed et al., 2017; Visscher et al., 2008) but close to 700 variants found in an analysis based on more than 250,000 individuals only explain 20% of this total heritability (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the explained heritability of human height.

claim: Multiple justifications for missing heritability have been suggested, including the presence of low-frequency variants, structural variants, small effect variants, and low power to estimate non-additive effects.
source: Multiple justifications for this so-called missing heritability have been suggested, including the presence of low-frequency variants, (Gibson, 2012; Hindorff et al., 2009; Manolio et al., 2009; Pritchard, 2001; Walter et al., 2015), structural variants (e.g. copy number variants) (Peter et al., 2018), small effect variants, as well as the low power to estimate non-additive effects (Cordell, 2009; Mackay, 2014; Zuk et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies discussing potential explanations for missing heritability.

claim: Variants present in less than 5% of the individuals are coined as low-frequency variants.
source: Variants present in less than 5% of the individuals are coined as low-frequency variants and are known to be involved in a large number of rare Mendelian disorders (Gibson, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript defines low-frequency variants and cites a study on their involvement in disorders.

claim: Low-frequency variants are known to be involved in a large number of rare Mendelian disorders.
source: Variants present in less than 5% of the individuals are coined as low-frequency variants and are known to be involved in a large number of rare Mendelian disorders (Gibson, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the role of low-frequency variants in Mendelian disorders.

claim: Implication of rare variants is pervasive in common diseases and other complex traits.
source: However, implication of rare variants is also pervasive in common diseases and other complex traits.
evidence: The manuscript states the broader relevance of rare variants beyond Mendelian disorders.

claim: GWAS cannot deal with low-frequency and rare variants due to statistical limitations, except for very large sample sizes.
source: As GWAS cannot deal with low-frequency and rare variants due to statistical limitations, except for very large sample sizes, their effect has often been overlooked.
evidence: The manuscript explains the limitations of GWAS for detecting low-frequency variants.

claim: S. cerevisiae isolates can be found in a broad array of biotopes both human-associated and wild and are distributed world-wide.
source: S. cerevisiae isolates can be found in a broad array of biotopes both human-associated (e.g. wine, sake, beer and other fermented beverages, food, human body) or wild (e.g. plants, soil, insects) and are distributed world-wide (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ecological distribution of S. cerevisiae and cites a study.

claim: The S. cerevisiae species presents a high level of genetic diversity (π = 3×10−3), much greater than that found in humans.
source: Phenotypic diversity among yeast isolates is significant and the S. cerevisiae species presents a high level of genetic diversity (π = 3×10−3), much greater than that found in humans (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genetic diversity of S. cerevisiae and compares it to humans, citing a study.

claim: An unprecedented number of 1,011 S. cerevisiae natural isolates has been sequenced.
source: Because of their small and compact genomes, an unprecedented number of 1,011 S. cerevisiae natural isolates has recently been sequenced (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study that sequenced 1,011 yeast isolates.

claim: Yeast genome-wide association analyses have revealed functional Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs), explaining a small fraction of the phenotypic variance.
source: Yeast genome-wide association analyses have revealed functional Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs), explaining a small fraction of the phenotypic variance (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on yeast GWAS findings.

claim: Copy number variants (CNVs) account for a larger proportion of the phenotypic variance and have greater effects on phenotypes compared to SNPs in yeast.
source: However, these analyses highlighted the importance of the copy number variants (CNVs), which account for a larger proportion of the phenotypic variance and have greater effects on phenotypes compared to the SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript describes findings about CNVs from previous yeast GWAS studies.

claim: Even when CNVs and SNPs are taken together, the phenotypic variance explained is still low (approximately 17% on average) in yeast.
source: Nevertheless, even when CNVs and SNPs are taken together, the phenotypic variance explained is still low (approximately 17% on average) and consequently a large part of it is unexplained.
evidence: The manuscript reports the combined variance explained by CNVs and SNPs from previous studies.

claim: There was a near perfect correlation (Pearson's r = 0.995, p-value<2.2e-16) between expected and observed phenotypic values in the diallel model.
source: We found a near perfect correlation (Pearson's r = 0.995, p-value<2.2e-16) between expected and observed phenotypic values, confirming the accuracy of the model used (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation between model predictions and observations.

claim: The overall correlation between the MATa and MATα parental strains was 0.967 (Pearson, p-value<1e-324).
source: The overall correlation between the MATa and MATα parental strains was 0.967 (Pearson, p-value<1e-324), with an average correlation per strain of 0.976 across different conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation between mating types.

claim: The average correlation per strain between MATa and MATα was 0.976 across different conditions.
source: The overall correlation between the MATa and MATα parental strains was 0.967 (Pearson, p-value<1e-324), with an average correlation per strain of 0.976 across different conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the average per-strain correlation between mating types.

claim: No significant mating type specificity was identified.
source: No significant mating type specificity was identified.
evidence: The manuscript reports the conclusion from the mating type comparison.
